warmup.q: open class Base { fun amount(c: Long): Base = this } and class Card : Base() { fun token(t: String): Card = this }. Which chain compiles?
options: Both, because the object is a Card either way
warmup.why: Each call returns its declared type. token returns a Card, so amount can follow. amount returns a Base, and Base has no token, even though the object is really a Card. The compiler goes by static types, which is the problem self types solve.

sections.h: A self type lets base-class setters return the subclass
sections.html:
Builders are where the plain generics of lessons 1 to 9 stop being enough. Put the common setters in a base class, add a subclass with its own setter, and the chain breaks as soon as a base setter runs:

Java
class PlainBuilder {
    protected long cents;
    PlainBuilder amount(long cents) { this.cents = cents; return this; }
}
class PlainCardBuilder extends PlainBuilder {
    PlainCardBuilder cardToken(String t) { ... }
}

new PlainCardBuilder().amount(1_200).cardToken("tok_1");   // error: cannot find symbol
Kotlin
open class PlainBuilder {
    protected var cents = 0L
    fun amount(cents: Long): PlainBuilder { this.cents = cents; return this }
}
class PlainCardBuilder : PlainBuilder() {
    fun cardToken(t: String): PlainCardBuilder { ... }
}

PlainCardBuilder().amount(1_200).cardToken("tok_1")
// error: Unresolved reference 'cardToken' on receiver of type 'PlainBuilder'.

amount returns a PlainBuilder, because that's all the base class knows about itself. The object is still a PlainCardBuilder, but the static type has lost it. The base class needs a way to say "I return whatever subclass I really am". The answer is a self type, written as a recursive bound:

Java
abstract class Builder<B extends Builder<B>> {
    protected long cents;
    B amount(long cents) { this.cents = cents; return self(); }
    protected abstract B self();
}
final class CardBuilder extends Builder<CardBuilder> {
    CardBuilder cardToken(String t) { ...; return this; }
    @Override protected CardBuilder self() { return this; }
}
Kotlin
abstract class Builder<B : Builder<B>> {
    protected var cents = 0L
    fun amount(cents: Long): B { this.cents = cents; return self() }
    protected abstract fun self(): B
}
class CardBuilder : Builder<CardBuilder>() {
    fun cardToken(t: String): CardBuilder { ...; return this }
    override fun self() = this
}

Read B : Builder<B> as "B is a builder whose own B is B". The only types that fit are subclasses that name themselves, as CardBuilder : Builder<CardBuilder>() does. Inside the base class, B stands for "my concrete subclass", so amount can return it. You met the shape already: lesson 2's T : Comparable<T> is a recursive bound, and Java's own Enum<E extends Enum<E>> is one too.

Two details matter. The abstract self() keeps the code checked: each subclass returns this, and the compiler verifies it is a B. And the bound can't force honesty: class Liar : Builder<CardBuilder>() compiles. If you write self() as abstract, the liar must return a CardBuilder it doesn't have, which is where you'd notice.

In pure Kotlin code you often don't need a builder at all. A data class with default arguments and copy covers most cases. Reach for self types when Java callers need a builder, or when you extend a Java class that already uses one.

figure.caption: A recursive bound lets the base class return its concrete subclass, so a chain keeps the subclass's own setters in reach.

try.title: Break a builder chain, then fix it with B : Builder<B>
steps: Run SelfTypeDemo (or SelfTypeDemoJava). Compare the static type and the run-time class on the first line.
Uncomment wrong move 2, the Liar class. It compiles. Add println(Liar().amount(5)::class.simpleName) below it and predict what prints.

code.title: SelfTypeDemo.kt
code.html: package workbench.generics.l10.demo // 1. Without a self type: the base setters return the base class, and the chain loses the subclass. open class PlainBuilder { protected var cents = 0L fun amount(cents: Long): PlainBuilder { this.cents = cents; return this } } class PlainCardBuilder : PlainBuilder() { private var token = "" fun cardToken(t: String): PlainCardBuilder { token = t; return this } fun build() = "card $cents with $token" } // 2. With a self type: B names "my own subclass", so the base setters return it. abstract class Builder<B : Builder<B>> { protected var cents = 0L fun amount(cents: Long): B { this.cents = cents; return self() } protected abstract fun self(): B } class CardBuilder : Builder<CardBuilder>() { private var token = "" fun cardToken(t: String): CardBuilder { token = t; return this } override fun self() = this fun build() = "card $cents with $token" } fun main() { val lost: PlainBuilder = PlainCardBuilder().cardToken("tok_1").amount(1_200) // amount() returns a PlainBuilder println("after amount(): static type PlainBuilder, run-time class ${lost::class.simpleName}") println(CardBuilder().amount(1_200).cardToken("tok_1").build()) // the chain keeps CardBuilder // Wrong moves. Uncomment one at a time, predict the error, then run. // println(PlainCardBuilder().amount(1_200).cardToken("tok_1").build()) // 1 // class Liar : Builder<CardBuilder>() { override fun self() = CardBuilder() } // 2 (compiles: what does it break?) }

The same recursive bound that java.lang.Enum uses: Enum<E extends Enum<E>>. */ public class SelfTypeDemoJava { static class PlainBuilder { protected long cents; PlainBuilder amount(long cents) { this.cents = cents; return this; } } static final class PlainCardBuilder extends PlainBuilder { private String token = ""; PlainCardBuilder cardToken(String t) { token = t; return this; } String build() { return "card " + cents + " with " + token; } } static abstract class Builder<B extends Builder<B>> { protected long cents; B amount(long cents) { this.cents = cents; return self(); } protected abstract B self(); } static final class CardBuilder extends Builder<CardBuilder> { private String token = ""; CardBuilder cardToken(String t) { token = t; return this; } @Override protected CardBuilder self() { return this; } String build() { return "card " + cents + " with " + token; } } public static void main(String[] args) { PlainBuilder lost = new PlainCardBuilder().cardToken("tok_1").amount(1_200); // amount() returns a PlainBuilder System.out.println("after amount(): static type PlainBuilder, run-time class " + lost.getClass().getSimpleName()); System.out.println(new CardBuilder().amount(1_200).cardToken("tok_1").build()); // Wrong move. Uncomment, predict the error, then run. // System.out.println(new PlainCardBuilder().amount(1_200).cardToken("tok_1").build()); } }

try.expect: Both print after amount(): static type PlainBuilder, run-time class PlainCardBuilder and card 1200 with tok_1. Wrong move 1 fails with Unresolved reference 'cardToken' on receiver of type 'PlainBuilder'. (Java: cannot find symbol). The Liar compiles because the bound only asks for some builder, and Liar().amount(5) prints CardBuilder: a fresh object, not the liar you configured. Nothing forces a subclass to pass itself.

sections.h: T & Any says definitely not null
sections.html:
The default bound of a type parameter is Any? (lesson 2), so a plain T may be a nullable type. Sometimes you know that one particular value is not null, and you want the type to say so. Kotlin writes that as T & Any, a definitely non-nullable type: "T, with null taken out".

Java
// Java's types say nothing about null. The best you can do is a comment and a run-time check.
static <T> T firstNotNullValue(List<T> items) {
    for (T item : items) if (item != null) return item;
    throw new NoSuchElementException("no non-null element");
}

String first = firstNotNullValue(Arrays.asList(null, "eur", "usd"));
Kotlin
fun <T> List<T>.firstNotNullValue(): T & Any {
    for (item in this) if (item != null) return item     // smart cast: item is T & Any here
    throw NoSuchElementException("no non-null element")
}

val first: String = listOf(null, "eur", "usd").firstNotNullValue()   // T = String?, result String

With T = String?, T & Any is String. With T = Payment, it's Payment. The compiler holds you to it: returning a plain T gives Return type mismatch: expected 'T (of fun <T> forget) & Any', actual 'T (of fun <T> forget)'.

The Kotlin docs name the main use case: overriding Java methods whose generic parameters are annotated @NotNull. Kotlin reads @NotNull T in a Java interface as T & Any:

Java
public interface NotNullTransformer<T> {
    @NotNull T transform(@NotNull T value);
}
Kotlin
class UpperCaser<T : CharSequence?> : NotNullTransformer<T> {
    override fun transform(value: T & Any): T & Any = ...
}

Two rules come with it. The left side must be a type parameter with a nullable bound; with T : Any there is no null to remove, and the compiler says Intersection types are supported only for definitely non-nullable types: left part must be a type parameter with nullable bounds. And the guarantee is Kotlin-only: Java sees <T> T firstNotNullValue(List<T>) with no trace of & Any.

The docs also say that when you work only with Kotlin, you'll rarely need to write it, because inference handles it. Expect to type T & Any at the Java boundary and in small helpers. One more that earns its keep in a message handler:

Java
// Java: the null check happens, but the type can't record it
static <T> T requireValue(T value, String name) {
    if (value == null) throw new IllegalArgumentException(name + " is required");
    return value;
}
Kotlin
fun <T> T.requireValue(name: String): T & Any = this ?: throw IllegalArgumentException("$name is required")

val token: String = message.cardToken.requireValue("card token")   // cardToken is a String?

It turns an optional field of a Kafka message into a value the rest of the handler can use without !!.

try.title: Take null out of a type
steps: Run NonNullDemo (or NonNullDemoJava). Open NotNullTransformer.java next to it: a Java interface with @NotNull.
Uncomment wrong moves 1 and 2 in NonNullDemo.kt one at a time. Predict first.
Uncomment function 3 at the bottom. In the Java twin, uncomment the oops line and run: what does Java catch, and when?

code.title: NonNullDemo.kt
code.html: package workbench.generics.l10.demo /** T may be nullable (String?), but the result is "T, definitely not null". */ fun <T> List<T>.firstNotNullValue(): T & Any { for (item in this) if (item != null) return item // smart cast: item is T & Any here throw NoSuchElementException("no non-null element") } /** The docs' example: fall back to a value that is known not to be null. */ fun <T> elvis(x: T, y: T & Any): T & Any = x ?: y /** Implements the Java interface in NonNullDemoJava.java, whose methods are annotated @NotNull. */ class UpperCaser<T : CharSequence?> : NotNullTransformer<T> { @Suppress("UNCHECKED_CAST") override fun transform(value: T & Any): T & Any = value.toString().uppercase() as (T & Any) } fun main() { val currencies: List<String?> = listOf(null, "eur", "usd") val first: String = currencies.firstNotNullValue() // T = String?, result String val note: String? = null val shown: String = elvis(note, "no note") println("first = $first, shown = $shown") println("transformed = ${UpperCaser<String?>().transform("pay_1")}") // Wrong moves. Uncomment one at a time, predict the error, then run. // fun <T> forget(x: T): T & Any = x // 1 // val n: String = UpperCaser<String?>().transform(null) // 2 } // 3. & Any needs a type parameter whose bound is nullable. // fun <T : Any> pointless(x: T & Any) {}

alt.title: NonNullDemoJava.java
alt.html: package workbench.generics.l10.demo; import java.util.Arrays; import java.util.List; import java.util.NoSuchElementException; import java.util.Objects; /** * Java twin of NonNullDemo.kt. Java types say nothing about null, so "T, but not null" can only be * a convention (or an annotation such as @NotNull), checked at run time. */ public class NonNullDemoJava { static <T> T firstNotNullValue(List<T> items) { for (T item : items) if (item != null) return item; throw new NoSuchElementException("no non-null element"); } static <T> T elvis(T x, T y) { return x != null ? x : Objects.requireNonNull(y); } public static void main(String[] args) { List<String> currencies = Arrays.asList(null, "eur", "usd"); String first = firstNotNullValue(currencies); String shown = elvis(null, "no note"); System.out.println("first = " + first + ", shown = " + shown); System.out.println("transformed = " + new UpperCaser<String>().transform("pay_1")); // Uncomment and run: it compiles in Java. What happens at run time? // String oops = elvis(null, null); } }

try.expect: Both print first = eur, shown = no note and transformed = PAY_1. Kotlin's wrong moves: (1) Return type mismatch: expected 'T (of fun <T> forget) & Any', actual 'T (of fun <T> forget)'., (2) Null cannot be a value of a non-null type 'String'.: for T = String?, T & Any is String. Function 3: Intersection types are supported only for definitely non-nullable types: left part must be a type parameter with nullable bounds. The Java oops line compiles and throws NullPointerException from Objects.requireNonNull at run time.

sections.h: @UnsafeVariance: how List<out E> can take an E in contains
sections.html:
Here is a puzzle from lesson 4. List is declared interface List<out E>, and an out parameter can't appear in a parameter position. Yet you call list.contains(x) every day. The standard library's source (2.4.21) shows how:

public operator fun contains(element: @UnsafeVariance E): Boolean
public fun indexOf(element: @UnsafeVariance E): Int

@UnsafeVariance "suppresses errors about variance conflict" for one type use. It is a promise from the author: this parameter is only compared, never stored, so a List<Int> seen as a List<Number> can't be damaged by it. contains(2.5) on that list just returns false.

Why take an E at all, when Any? would need no annotation? Because the E lets the compiler catch nonsense checks. Java chose Object, and pays for it:

Java
Set<Long> paymentIds = Set.of(42L);
paymentIds.contains(42);                      // false: 42 is boxed to an Integer, and Integer(42) != Long(42)
List.of(1_200, 350).contains("1200");         // compiles, always false
Kotlin
val paymentIds: Set<Long> = setOf(42L)
paymentIds.contains(42)                       // true: the literal 42 is typed as a Long here
listOf(1_200, 350).contains("1200")
// error: Type inference failed. The value of the type parameter 'T' must be mentioned in input types ...

That first Java line is a real bug class: an int payment id looked up in a set of Longs, false every time.

The annotation is called unsafe for a reason. It switches the check off, and the compiler believes you:

Java
// Java's way to break a ? extends view on purpose is an unchecked cast:
List<? extends Object> view = ids;
((List<Object>) view).add(42);
String lastId = ids.get(ids.size() - 1);      // ClassCastException
Kotlin
class Ledger<out T>(first: T) {
    private val entries = mutableListOf(first)
    fun add(entry: @UnsafeVariance T) { entries.add(entry) }   // stores it: a broken promise
    fun last(): T = entries.last()
}

val ids: Ledger<String> = Ledger("pay_1")
val anything: Ledger<Any> = ids               // fine: Ledger is out T
anything.add(42)                              // compiles
val lastId: String = ids.last()               // ClassCastException

Use @UnsafeVariance only on parameters that are read and compared (contains, indexOf, an equality check), never on ones that are kept. You might write it yourself on a read-only covariant type that offers a lookup, such as interface Page<out T> { fun indexOf(item: @UnsafeVariance T): Int }. To check that it's honest, follow the parameter through the body. If it only reaches ==, equals or hashCode, the promise holds. If it reaches a field, a collection or a callback that keeps it, remove the annotation and make the type invariant, or split it into a read view and a write view, as lesson 11 of this track does.

steps: Run UnsafeVarianceDemo and UnsafeVarianceDemoJava. Find the line that compiles in Java and is rejected in Kotlin.

It is a lie. */ class Ledger<out T>(first: T) { private val entries = mutableListOf(first) fun add(entry: @UnsafeVariance T) { entries.add(entry) } fun last(): T = entries.last() } fun main() { // 1. The standard library uses @UnsafeVariance safely: contains only compares, it never stores. val amounts: List<Number> = listOf(1_200, 350) // List<Int> seen as List<Number> println("contains(350): ${amounts.contains(350)}, contains(2.5): ${amounts.contains(2.5)}") // 2. And because contains takes an E, the compiler can catch a nonsense check. // println(listOf(1_200, 350).contains("1200")) // wrong move 1 // 3. Used carelessly, the same annotation breaks type safety. val ids: Ledger<String> = Ledger("pay_1") val anything: Ledger<Any> = ids // fine: Ledger is out T anything.add(42) // compiles thanks to @UnsafeVariance try { val lastId: String = ids.last() println(lastId) } catch (e: ClassCastException) { println("ClassCastException: ${e.message?.substringBefore(" (")}") } } // Wrong move 2: remove @UnsafeVariance from a copy of Ledger and read the error. // class Ledger2<out T> { fun add(entry: T) {} }

alt.html: package workbench.generics.l10.demo; import java.util.ArrayList; import java.util.List; /** * Java twin of UnsafeVarianceDemo.kt. Java's contains takes an Object, so it never needed the * annotation, and it can't catch a nonsense check. Java's way to break a ? extends view on purpose * is an unchecked cast. */ public class UnsafeVarianceDemoJava { @SuppressWarnings("unchecked") public static void main(String[] args) { List<? extends Number> amounts = List.of(1_200, 350); System.out.println("contains(350): " + amounts.contains(350) + ", contains(2.5): " + amounts.contains(2.5)); System.out.println("contains(\"1200\") compiles in Java: " + List.of(1_200, 350).contains("1200")); List<String> ids = new ArrayList<>(List.of("pay_1")); List<? extends Object> view = ids; ((List<Object>) view).add(42); // the unchecked cast is the Java "unsafe variance" try { String lastId = ids.get(ids.size() - 1); System.out.println(lastId); } catch (ClassCastException e) { System.out.println("ClassCastException: " + e.getMessage().split(" \\(")[0]); } } }

The value of the type parameter 'T' must be mentioned in input types ..., and Ledger2 fails with Type parameter 'T' is declared as 'out' but occurs in 'in' position in type 'T (of class Ledger2<out T>)'.

sections.h: Function types, Nothing and type aliases
sections.html:
Three more tools sit at the edges of the type system.

Function types carry variance on both ends. (P) -> R is Function1<in P, out R> (lesson 5), so a composition helper accepts a more general second step and can hand back a more general result:

Java
// Function<T, R> is invariant, so the JDK writes the variance into the signature:
// default <V> Function<T, V> andThen(Function<? super R, ? extends V> after)
Function<String, Long> parseCents = s -> Long.parseLong(s.replace(".", ""));
Function<Object, String> describe = x -> "<" + x + ">";
Function<String, String> pipeline = parseCents.andThen(describe);      // <1250> for "12.50"
Kotlin
fun <A, B, C> andThen(first: (A) -> B, second: (B) -> C): (A) -> C = { a -> second(first(a)) }

val parseCents: (String) -> Long = { it.replace(".", "").toLong() }
val describe: (Any) -> String = { "<$it>" }                  // takes Any, not just Long
val pipeline: (String) -> CharSequence = andThen(parseCents, describe)   // <1250> for "12.50"

Nothing is the bottom type: a subtype of every type, with no values at all. throw and TODO() have type Nothing, which is why val strict: Long = text.toLongOrNull() ?: fail("not a number") type-checks when fun fail(reason: String): Nothing. It also explains emptyList(): one shared List<Nothing> fits every List<Payment>, because List is out E and Nothing is below Payment. Lesson 11 uses the same trick for Either. Java has no bottom type. Collections.emptyList() is a generic method whose T is inferred at each call, and a Kotlin List<Nothing> reaches Java as a raw List.

A type alias gives an existing type a shorter name, and it can be generic:

Java
// Java has no type aliases. The nearest thing, a functional interface, is a new, separate type.
@FunctionalInterface interface Handler<E> { void handle(E event); }
Kotlin
typealias Handler<E> = (E) -> Unit           // just a name: a Handler<E> IS an (E) -> Unit
typealias Table<K> = MutableMap<K, MutableList<K>>

val audit: Handler<CardAuthorized> = { println("audit ${it.paymentId}") }
val plain: (CardAuthorized) -> Unit = audit  // same type, no conversion

Because an alias is only a name, it has the variance of what it stands for: a Handler<PaymentEvent> is a Handler<CardAuthorized>, exactly as with the function type. Aliases nested inside a class became Stable in Kotlin 2.3, with one limit: they can't mention the outer class's type parameters.

try.title: Compose with variance, fail with Nothing
steps: Run FunctionTypesDemo (or FunctionTypesDemoJava, which also calls the JDK's own andThen).
Uncomment the wrong move and read which type the compiler inferred for the pipeline.
Change fail's return type from Nothing to Unit. Which line breaks, and why?

code.title: FunctionTypesDemo.kt
code.html: package workbench.generics.l10.demo /** A new name for a function type. Not a new type: a Handler<E> IS an (E) -> Unit. */ typealias Handler<E> = (E) -> Unit fun <A, B, C> andThen(first: (A) -> B, second: (B) -> C): (A) -> C = { a -> second(first(a)) } fun fail(reason: String): Nothing = throw IllegalArgumentException(reason) fun main() { // 1. Function1<in P, out R>: a more general second function fits. val parseCents: (String) -> Long = { it.replace(".", "").toLong() } val describe: (Any) -> String = { "<$it>" } val pipeline: (String) -> CharSequence = andThen(parseCents, describe) println("pipeline(\"12.50\") = ${pipeline("12.50")}") // 2. Nothing is a subtype of every type. val none: List<CardAuth> = emptyList() // emptyList() is a List<Nothing> here val cents: Long = "x".toLongOrNull() ?: 0L val strict: Long = "1200".toLongOrNull() ?: fail("not a number") // fail returns Nothing, so this is a Long println("none = $none, cents = $cents, strict = $strict") // 3. A type alias is only a name. val audit: Handler<CardAuth> = { println("audit ${it.id}") } val plain: (CardAuth) -> Unit = audit // same type, no conversion plain(CardAuth("pay_1")) // Wrong move. Uncomment, predict the error, then run. // val tooStrict: (Any) -> String = andThen(parseCents, describe) } data class CardAuth(val id: String)

alt.title: FunctionTypesDemoJava.java
alt.html: package workbench.generics.l10.demo; import java.util.Collections; import java.util.List; import java.util.function.Consumer; import java.util.function.Function; /** * Java twin of FunctionTypesDemo.kt. Java's Function<T, R> is invariant, so the JDK writes the * variance into andThen's signature: andThen(Function<? super R, ? extends V> after). */ public class FunctionTypesDemoJava { static <A, B, C> Function<A, C> andThen(Function<A, ? extends B> first, Function<? super B, ? extends C> second) { return a -> second.apply(first.apply(a)); } static <T> T fail(String reason) { throw new IllegalArgumentException(reason); } // no Nothing: fake it with T public static void main(String[] args) { Function<String, Long> parseCents = s -> Long.parseLong(s.replace(".", "")); Function<Object, String> describe = x -> "<" + x + ">"; Function<String, CharSequence> pipeline = andThen(parseCents, describe); System.out.println("pipeline(\"12.50\") = " + pipeline.apply("12.50")); System.out.println("JDK andThen: " + parseCents.andThen(describe).apply("3.50")); List<CardAuth> none = Collections.emptyList(); // generic method: T inferred as CardAuth long strict = Long.parseLong("1200"); System.out.println("none = " + none + ", strict = " + strict); Consumer<CardAuth> audit = a -> System.out.println("audit " + a.getId()); // no type aliases in Java audit.accept(new CardAuth("pay_1")); } }

try.expect: Kotlin prints pipeline("12.50") = <1250>, none = [], cents = 0, strict = 1200 and audit pay_1; Java prints the same plus JDK andThen: <350>. The wrong move fails with Initializer type mismatch: expected '(Any) -> String', actual '(String) -> String'.: a function that needs a String input can't stand in for one that takes Any. With Unit, the strict line fails with Initializer type mismatch: expected 'Long', actual 'Any'.: the elvis expression's type becomes the common supertype of Long and Unit. Nothing fits there because it is a subtype of Long.

analogy: A self type is like a franchise operations manual. Head office writes it once, and every step ends with "hand the tray back to the counter of ______". When a restaurant joins, it writes its own name in the blank: that's CardBuilder : Builder<CardBuilder>(). Every franchise then gets a manual that sends trays back to its own counter, without head office knowing any franchise by name. The analogy breaks in the same place the code does: a franchise could write another restaurant's name in the blank, and the manual can't stop it. The recursive bound only checks that the name belongs to some franchise.
world: You meet self types in Java libraries before you write one. Testcontainers declares GenericContainer<SELF extends GenericContainer<SELF>>, which is why Kotlin test code for an Oracle or Kafka integration test sometimes needs class KGenericContainer(image: String) : GenericContainer<KGenericContainer>(image) just to use the fluent withEnv(...) chain. Card-issuer and banking SDKs in Java often ship builder hierarchies with the same shape. T & Any shows up when your Kotlin code implements a Java interface from such an SDK that marks generic parameters @NotNull. And Nothing is the honest return type for helpers like fun rejectPayment(reason: String): Nothing in a Temporal activity, which lets val card = request.card ?: rejectPayment("no card") type-check without a dummy value.
mistake: The common mistake in self-typed builders is the unchecked shortcut: @Suppress("UNCHECKED_CAST") fun amount(c: Long): B { cents = c; return this as B } in the base class, with no self(). It works until someone copies a subclass and forgets to change the type argument: class WalletBuilder : Builder<CardBuilder>(). That compiles, and WalletBuilder().amount(5) throws ClassCastException: class WalletBuilder cannot be cast to class CardBuilder at the call site, because erasure made the cast inside amount check nothing. People write the cast because it saves one override per subclass. The fix is an abstract protected abstract fun self(): B that each subclass implements as = this. Then the same copy-paste slip is a compile error: Return type mismatch: expected 'CardPaymentBuilder', actual 'WalletPaymentBuilder'.

compare.title: A self-typed builder hierarchy in Java and Kotlin

java.title: PaymentRequestBuilder.java
java.html: abstract class PaymentRequestBuilder<B extends PaymentRequestBuilder<B>> { protected long cents; protected String currency; B amount(long cents) { this.cents = cents; return self(); } B currency(String code) { this.currency = code; return self(); } protected abstract B self(); } final class CardPaymentBuilder extends PaymentRequestBuilder<CardPaymentBuilder> { private String token; CardPaymentBuilder cardToken(String token) { this.token = token; return this; } @Override protected CardPaymentBuilder self() { return this; } CardPayment build() { if (cents <= 0) throw new IllegalStateException("amount must be positive"); return new CardPayment(cents, currency, "", token); } } // new CardPaymentBuilder().amount(1_200).currency("EUR").cardToken("tok_42").build();

kotlin.title: PaymentRequestBuilder.kt
kotlin.html: abstract class PaymentRequestBuilder<B : PaymentRequestBuilder<B>> { protected var cents: Long = 0 protected var currency: String? = null fun amount(cents: Long): B { this.cents = cents; return self() } fun currency(code: String): B { currency = code; return self() } protected abstract fun self(): B } class CardPaymentBuilder : PaymentRequestBuilder<CardPaymentBuilder>() { private var token: String? = null fun cardToken(token: String): CardPaymentBuilder { this.token = token; return this } override fun self() = this fun build(): CardPayment { check(cents > 0) { "amount must be positive" } return CardPayment(cents, currency!!, "", checkNotNull(token)) } } // CardPaymentBuilder().amount(1_200).currency("EUR").cardToken("tok_42").build()

compare.note: The recursive bound is the same idea in both languages: B extends PaymentRequestBuilder<B> and B : PaymentRequestBuilder<B>, with each subclass passing itself and an abstract self() instead of an unchecked cast. Kotlin adds checks Java can't express: currency is a String?, so build() must deal with a missing value, and helpers like check and checkNotNull throw IllegalStateException with your message. The other three tools of this lesson have no Java twin: T & Any (Java types carry no nullability), @UnsafeVariance (Java has no declaration-site variance to suppress), and Nothing (Java has no bottom type). Java also has no type aliases. And in Kotlin you can often skip the builder entirely with a data class, default arguments and copy.

worked.title: Add a wallet payment to the builder hierarchy

steps.say: The lab's hierarchy has card payments and bank transfers. Product wants wallet payments too. The quickest path is copy and paste from CardPaymentBuilder, and that's how the classic bug gets in: the type argument still says CardPaymentBuilder.
steps.code: class WalletPaymentBuilder : PaymentRequestBuilder<CardPaymentBuilder>() { // copied, not changed private var walletId: String? = null fun walletId(id: String): WalletPaymentBuilder { walletId = id; return this } override fun self(): CardPaymentBuilder = this } // error: Return type mismatch: expected 'CardPaymentBuilder', actual 'WalletPaymentBuilder'.

alt.html: final class WalletPaymentBuilder extends PaymentRequestBuilder<CardPaymentBuilder> { // copied, not changed private String walletId; WalletPaymentBuilder walletId(String id) { walletId = id; return this; } @Override protected CardPaymentBuilder self() { return this; } } // error: incompatible types: WalletPaymentBuilder cannot be converted to CardPaymentBuilder

steps.say: 1. The abstract self() caught it at compile time. With return this as B in the base class it would have compiled and failed later, at the first amount(...) call. Fix the declaration: the subclass passes itself.
steps.code: class WalletPaymentBuilder : PaymentRequestBuilder<WalletPaymentBuilder>() { private var walletId: String? = null fun walletId(id: String): WalletPaymentBuilder { walletId = id; return this } override fun self() = this // B is WalletPaymentBuilder: no cast

alt.html: final class WalletPaymentBuilder extends PaymentRequestBuilder<WalletPaymentBuilder> { private String walletId; WalletPaymentBuilder walletId(String id) { walletId = id; return this; } @Override protected WalletPaymentBuilder self() { return this; } // no cast

steps.say: 1. Build: check the common fields with the base class's checkCommon(), then the wallet's own field. Self-check: why does amount(...) in the chain below return a WalletPaymentBuilder without any change to the base class? (Because B is filled with WalletPaymentBuilder in the declaration, and amount returns B.)
steps.code: fun build(): WalletPayment { checkCommon() val id = checkNotNull(walletId) { "wallet id is required" } return WalletPayment(cents, currency!!, reference, id) } } val p = WalletPaymentBuilder().amount(2_500).currency("EUR").walletId("wal_9").build()

alt.html: WalletPayment build() { checkCommon(); if (walletId == null) throw new IllegalStateException("wallet id is required"); return new WalletPayment(cents, currency, reference, walletId); } } WalletPayment p = new WalletPaymentBuilder().amount(2_500).currency("EUR").walletId("wal_9").build();

lab.title: A self-typed builder hierarchy, and functions with variance
steps: Run the tests. All eight fail. The signatures are done; read them first, especially PaymentRequestBuilder<B : PaymentRequestBuilder<B>> and the two subclass declarations.
In Builders.kt, write the three base setters: store the value, then return self(). Write checkCommon() with two check(...) calls.
Write self(), the setter and build() in CardPaymentBuilder and BankTransferBuilder. build() calls checkCommon() first, then checks its own field.
In Functions.kt, write andThen as a lambda, and fanOut as a lambda that calls each handler in order. Read the fanOut test: it passes a Handler<PaymentEvent> where Handler<CardAuthorized> is expected.
Write firstNotNullValue with a loop. Notice that returning the smart-cast item satisfies T & Any.
Run the tests until all eight pass.
hints: fun amount(cents: Long): B { this.cents = cents; return self() } is the whole pattern for each setter.
checkNotNull(token) { "card token is required" } returns the non-null value or throws IllegalStateException with that message.
andThen is one line: = { a -> second(first(a)) }. fanOut is = { event -> for (h in handlers) h(event) }.

drill.title: Write a self-typed builder from memory
drill.prompt: Close this page. Write an abstract Builder with a recursive bound, one setter amount(cents) that returns the subclass type, and an abstract self(). Then write CardBuilder with cardToken(t) and build(), so that CardBuilder().amount(1_200).cardToken("tok_1").build() compiles. Do it in Kotlin, then in Java.

answer.html: abstract class Builder<B : Builder<B>> { protected var cents = 0L fun amount(cents: Long): B { this.cents = cents; return self() } protected abstract fun self(): B } class CardBuilder : Builder<CardBuilder>() { // the subclass fills B with itself private var token = "" fun cardToken(t: String): CardBuilder { token = t; return this } override fun self() = this fun build() = "card $cents with $token" }

alt.title: Builder.java
alt.html: abstract class Builder<B extends Builder<B>> { protected long cents; B amount(long cents) { this.cents = cents; return self(); } protected abstract B self(); } final class CardBuilder extends Builder<CardBuilder> { // the subclass fills B with itself private String token = ""; CardBuilder cardToken(String t) { token = t; return this; } @Override protected CardBuilder self() { return this; } String build() { return "card " + cents + " with " + token; } }

recap: A recursive bound, B : Builder<B>, lets a base class name its own concrete subclass, so base setters can return it and chains keep subclass methods.
Each subclass passes itself (CardBuilder : Builder<CardBuilder>()) and implements an abstract self() = this. Avoid this as B: it is unchecked and fails late.
T & Any is "T without null": for T = String? it's String. Its main use is overriding Java generic methods marked @NotNull.
List<out E> declares contains(element: @UnsafeVariance E). That's safe because contains only compares, and the E lets Kotlin reject listOf(1).contains("1").
@UnsafeVariance on a parameter that gets stored breaks type safety and ends in a ClassCastException.
Nothing is a subtype of every type, so emptyList() fits any List<T> and ?: fail(...) type-checks. A type alias is only a new name, with the variance of the type it names.

explain.prompt: A teammate sees abstract class PaymentRequestBuilder<B : PaymentRequestBuilder<B>> in a code review and says it looks circular and pointless. Explain in your own words what problem it solves, how a subclass uses it, and what it can't prevent.
explain.answer: Without it, a setter in the base class can only return the base class type, so after calling amount() on a CardPaymentBuilder the compiler thinks it has a plain builder and won't let you call cardToken(). The recursive bound gives the base class a name, B, for "whatever concrete subclass I am". Each subclass fills it in with itself, as in class CardPaymentBuilder : PaymentRequestBuilder<CardPaymentBuilder>(), so inside that subclass B means CardPaymentBuilder and every inherited setter returns that type. The bound only looks circular: it reads "B is a builder whose B is B", which only self-naming subclasses satisfy. Each subclass implements self() as this, which the compiler checks, so no unchecked cast is needed. What it can't prevent is a subclass passing the wrong class, such as a wallet builder that says PaymentRequestBuilder<CardPaymentBuilder>. The abstract self() turns that into a compile error, which is why it's better than this as B.

deeper.html:
Recursive bounds go further than builders. java.lang.Enum is declared Enum<E extends Enum<E>> so that compareTo takes the same enum type, and EnumSet.noneOf(Class<E>) is bounded <E extends Enum<E>>. Kotlin's Enum<E : Enum<E>> is the same declaration. Lesson 2's fun <T : Comparable<T>> maxOf2(a: T, b: T) is the most common recursive bound of all; the Java signature Kotlin generates for it is <T extends Comparable<? super T>>, because Kotlin's Comparable is declared in T.

The standard library's use of @UnsafeVariance is easy to check. In the 2.4.21 sources (kotlin-stdlib-sources.jar, file Collections.kt) it appears on contains, containsAll and indexOf of List, and on AbstractCollection.contains. The contains("1200") error you saw comes from a second safety net: when the member contains(element: Int) doesn't accept a String, the compiler tries the extension Iterable<T>.contains(element: T), whose T is marked so that it must match the receiver's element type, and inference fails with the message you read.

Two small facts about Nothing. The type of the literal null is Nothing?, which is why null fits every nullable type. And when a Kotlin function returns List<Nothing>, Java sees a raw List, because Java has no bottom type to write there.

Type aliases can't create the distinct types people sometimes want from them. typealias PaymentId = String lets you pass any String where a PaymentId is expected. If you want the compiler to keep payment ids and refund ids apart, use a value class, @JvmInline value class PaymentId(val value: String), which is a real type with no wrapper object at run time in most uses.
